A random variable is **discrete** when its values can be listed one by one (typically a count), and **continuous** when it can take every value in an interval (typically a measurement).

**(i) Number of unemployed graduates in a town of population 1 lakh.**

This is a count of people, so \(X\) is a **discrete** random variable.

Range \(= \{0, 1, 2, \ldots, 1{,}00{,}000\}\) (in practice bounded above by the number of graduates in the town).

**(ii) Amount of syrup prescribed by a physician.**

A quantity of liquid is measured, not counted, so \(X\) is a **continuous** random variable.

Range \(= \{x : x > 0,\ x \in \mathbb{R}\}\), i.e. the interval \((0, \infty)\), bounded above in practice by the largest dose prescribed.

**(iii) Gain in weight in a week of a person on a high-protein diet.**

Weight is a measurement, so \(X\) is a **continuous** random variable.

Range \(=\) an interval of real numbers. Read as a gain, the range is \([0, \infty)\); if a loss of weight is also to be allowed, \(X\) may be negative and the range is an interval of \(\mathbb{R}\) around \(0\).

**(iv) 5 rats selected from 20 rats of which 12 are male (so 8 are female); \(X =\) number of female rats selected.**

This is a count, so \(X\) is a **discrete** random variable.

The smallest value is \(0\), since all 5 could be chosen from the 12 males; the largest is \(5\), since \(8 \geq 5\) females are available.

Range \(= \{0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5\}\).

**(v) Speed (km/hr) of a car at a check post.**

Speed is a measurement, so \(X\) is a **continuous** random variable.

Range \(= \{x : x > 0,\ x \in \mathbb{R}\}\), i.e. the interval \((0, \infty)\), bounded above in practice by the maximum speed the car can attain.

**Summary.** (i) discrete, (ii) continuous, (iii) continuous, (iv) discrete, (v) continuous.

**(i) To find \(k\).**

For a p.m.f. we need \(P(X = x) \geq 0\) for every \(x\) **and** \(\sum P(X = x) = 1\).

\(\displaystyle\sum_{x=1}^{6} P(X = x) = k + 2k + 3k + 4k + 5k + 6k = 21k\)

\(\therefore\ 21k = 1\), so \(k = \dfrac{1}{21}\).

Since \(k = \dfrac{1}{21} > 0\), each of \(k, 2k, \ldots, 6k\) is positive, so both conditions hold and this is a genuine p.m.f.

The distribution is

| \(X = x\) | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 | 6 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| \(P(X = x)\) | \(\dfrac{1}{21}\) | \(\dfrac{2}{21}\) | \(\dfrac{3}{21}\) | \(\dfrac{4}{21}\) | \(\dfrac{5}{21}\) | \(\dfrac{6}{21}\) |

**(ii) The three probabilities.**

\(P(X \leq 4) = P(1) + P(2) + P(3) + P(4) = (1 + 2 + 3 + 4)k = 10k = \dfrac{10}{21}\)

The values of \(X\) are integers, so \(2 < X < 4\) means \(X = 3\) only:

\(P(2 < X < 4) = P(X = 3) = 3k = \dfrac{3}{21} = \dfrac{1}{7}\)

\(P(X \geq 3) = P(3) + P(4) + P(5) + P(6) = (3 + 4 + 5 + 6)k = 18k = \dfrac{18}{21} = \dfrac{6}{7}\)

\(\therefore\ k = \dfrac{1}{21}\), \(P(X \leq 4) = \dfrac{10}{21}\), \(P(2 < X < 4) = \dfrac{1}{7}\), \(P(X \geq 3) = \dfrac{6}{7}\).

First check that the table really is a p.m.f. Every entry is positive, and

\(\sum P(X = x) = 0.05 + 0.1 + 0.15 + 0.20 + 0.25 + 0.15 + 0.1 = 1\)

so it is valid.

**(i) \(X\) is positive**, i.e. \(X = 1, 2, 3\).

\(P(X > 0) = 0.25 + 0.15 + 0.1 = 0.5 = \dfrac{1}{2}\)

**(ii) \(X\) is non-negative**, i.e. \(X = 0, 1, 2, 3\).

\(P(X \geq 0) = 0.20 + 0.25 + 0.15 + 0.1 = 0.7 = \dfrac{7}{10}\)

**(iii) \(X\) is odd**, i.e. \(X = -3, -1, 1, 3\).

\(P(X \text{ is odd}) = 0.05 + 0.15 + 0.25 + 0.1 = 0.55 = \dfrac{11}{20}\)

**(iv) \(X\) is even**, i.e. \(X = -2, 0, 2\) (recall that \(0\) is an even number).

\(P(X \text{ is even}) = 0.1 + 0.20 + 0.15 = 0.45 = \dfrac{9}{20}\)

**Check.** Every value of \(X\) is either odd or even, and indeed \(0.55 + 0.45 = 1\).

\(\therefore\) (i) \(0.5\), (ii) \(0.7\), (iii) \(0.55\), (iv) \(0.45\).

**To find \(a\).**

For a p.m.f., \(\sum P(X = x) = 1\):

\(\dfrac{1}{20} + \dfrac{3}{20} + a + 2a + \dfrac{1}{20} = 1\)

\(\dfrac{5}{20} + 3a = 1\), so \(3a = 1 - \dfrac{1}{4} = \dfrac{3}{4}\)

\(\therefore\ a = \dfrac{1}{4} = \dfrac{5}{20}\)

Since \(a > 0\), all five probabilities are positive, so the table is a genuine p.m.f.:

| \(x\) | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| \(P(X = x)\) | \(\dfrac{1}{20}\) | \(\dfrac{3}{20}\) | \(\dfrac{5}{20}\) | \(\dfrac{10}{20}\) | \(\dfrac{1}{20}\) |

(Sum \(= \dfrac{1 + 3 + 5 + 10 + 1}{20} = \dfrac{20}{20} = 1\).)

**The c.d.f.** \(F(x) = P(X \leq x)\) is obtained by adding the probabilities cumulatively:

| \(x\) | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| \(F(x)\) | \(\dfrac{1}{20}\) | \(\dfrac{4}{20}\) | \(\dfrac{9}{20}\) | \(\dfrac{19}{20}\) | \(1\) |

Written as a step function,

\(F(x) = \begin{cases} 0, & x < 1 \\ \dfrac{1}{20}, & 1 \leq x < 2 \\ \dfrac{4}{20}, & 2 \leq x < 3 \\ \dfrac{9}{20}, & 3 \leq x < 4 \\ \dfrac{19}{20}, & 4 \leq x < 5 \\ 1, & x \geq 5 \end{cases}\)

As a c.d.f. must, \(F\) is non-decreasing and reaches \(1\) at the largest value of \(X\).

\(\therefore\ a = \dfrac{1}{4}\), and the c.d.f. is as tabulated above.

A fair coin is tossed 4 times, so the sample space has \(2^{4} = 16\) equally likely outcomes. Let \(X =\) number of heads obtained, so \(X\) takes the values \(0, 1, 2, 3, 4\).

Exactly \(x\) heads can occur in \({}^{4}C_{x}\) of the 16 outcomes, so

\(P(X = x) = \dfrac{{}^{4}C_{x}}{16}\)

Using \({}^{4}C_{0} = 1\), \({}^{4}C_{1} = 4\), \({}^{4}C_{2} = 6\), \({}^{4}C_{3} = 4\), \({}^{4}C_{4} = 1\), the probability distribution of \(X\) is

| \(X = x\) | 0 | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| \(P(X = x)\) | \(\dfrac{1}{16}\) | \(\dfrac{4}{16}\) | \(\dfrac{6}{16}\) | \(\dfrac{4}{16}\) | \(\dfrac{1}{16}\) |

Every entry is positive and the sum is \(\dfrac{1 + 4 + 6 + 4 + 1}{16} = \dfrac{16}{16} = 1\), so this is a valid p.m.f.

**Formula for the p.m.f.**

\(P(X = x) = \dfrac{{}^{4}C_{x}}{2^{4}} = \dfrac{{}^{4}C_{x}}{16}\), for \(x = 0, 1, 2, 3, 4\), and \(P(X = x) = 0\) otherwise.

A die is tossed twice, and the two tosses are independent.

**(i) Success \(=\) a number greater than 4.**

On one toss, "greater than 4" means 5 or 6, so

\(p = P(\text{success}) = \dfrac{2}{6} = \dfrac{1}{3}\), and \(q = 1 - p = \dfrac{2}{3}\)

Let \(X =\) number of successes in the two tosses, so \(X = 0, 1, 2\).

\(P(X = 0) = q^{2} = \left(\dfrac{2}{3}\right)^{2} = \dfrac{4}{9}\)

\(P(X = 1) = 2pq = 2 \times \dfrac{1}{3} \times \dfrac{2}{3} = \dfrac{4}{9}\)

\(P(X = 2) = p^{2} = \left(\dfrac{1}{3}\right)^{2} = \dfrac{1}{9}\)

| \(X = x\) | 0 | 1 | 2 |
|---|---|---|---|
| \(P(X = x)\) | \(\dfrac{4}{9}\) | \(\dfrac{4}{9}\) | \(\dfrac{1}{9}\) |

Sum \(= \dfrac{4 + 4 + 1}{9} = 1\), as required.

**(ii) Success \(=\) "six appears on at least one die".**

Here the success is defined for the **pair** of tosses, so the pair is one trial: the success either occurs or it does not, and \(X\) takes only the values \(0\) and \(1\).

The two tosses give \(6 \times 6 = 36\) equally likely outcomes. No six appears in \(5 \times 5 = 25\) of them, so

\(P(X = 0) = \dfrac{25}{36}\) and \(P(X = 1) = 1 - \dfrac{25}{36} = \dfrac{11}{36}\)

| \(X = x\) | 0 | 1 |
|---|---|---|
| \(P(X = x)\) | \(\dfrac{25}{36}\) | \(\dfrac{11}{36}\) |

Sum \(= \dfrac{25 + 11}{36} = 1\), as required.

**Note.** If instead one counted the number of sixes obtained in the two tosses, then \(p = \dfrac{1}{6}\) and the distribution would be \(\dfrac{25}{36}, \dfrac{10}{36}, \dfrac{1}{36}\) for \(X = 0, 1, 2\). But the question defines the success for the pair of dice, so the two-value table above is the required answer.

Throughout use \(E(X) = \sum x_{i}p_{i}\), \(\mathrm{Var}(X) = E\left(X^{2}\right) - \left[E(X)\right]^{2}\) and \(\sigma = \sqrt{\mathrm{Var}(X)}\).

**(i)** \(X = 1, 2, 3\) with probabilities \(\dfrac{1}{5}, \dfrac{2}{5}, \dfrac{2}{5}\) (which are positive and sum to \(1\)).

\(E(X) = 1 \times \dfrac{1}{5} + 2 \times \dfrac{2}{5} + 3 \times \dfrac{2}{5} = \dfrac{1 + 4 + 6}{5} = \dfrac{11}{5} = 2.2\)

\(E\left(X^{2}\right) = 1 \times \dfrac{1}{5} + 4 \times \dfrac{2}{5} + 9 \times \dfrac{2}{5} = \dfrac{1 + 8 + 18}{5} = \dfrac{27}{5} = 5.4\)

\(\mathrm{Var}(X) = \dfrac{27}{5} - \left(\dfrac{11}{5}\right)^{2} = \dfrac{135 - 121}{25} = \dfrac{14}{25} = 0.56\)

\(\sigma = \sqrt{\dfrac{14}{25}} = \dfrac{\sqrt{14}}{5} \approx 0.7483\)

**(ii)** \(X = -1, 0, 1\) with probabilities \(\dfrac{1}{5}, \dfrac{2}{5}, \dfrac{2}{5}\) (positive, sum \(= 1\)).

\(E(X) = (-1) \times \dfrac{1}{5} + 0 \times \dfrac{2}{5} + 1 \times \dfrac{2}{5} = \dfrac{-1 + 0 + 2}{5} = \dfrac{1}{5} = 0.2\)

\(E\left(X^{2}\right) = 1 \times \dfrac{1}{5} + 0 \times \dfrac{2}{5} + 1 \times \dfrac{2}{5} = \dfrac{1 + 0 + 2}{5} = \dfrac{3}{5} = 0.6\)

\(\mathrm{Var}(X) = \dfrac{3}{5} - \left(\dfrac{1}{5}\right)^{2} = \dfrac{15 - 1}{25} = \dfrac{14}{25} = 0.56\)

\(\sigma = \dfrac{\sqrt{14}}{5} \approx 0.7483\)

Note that the values here are exactly those of (i) reduced by \(2\). Shifting a random variable moves its mean but leaves its variance unchanged, which is precisely what the two answers show.

**(iii)** \(X = 1, 2, \ldots, n\), each with probability \(\dfrac{1}{n}\) (positive, and the sum is \(n \times \dfrac{1}{n} = 1\)).

\(E(X) = \dfrac{1}{n}\displaystyle\sum_{x=1}^{n} x = \dfrac{1}{n} \cdot \dfrac{n(n+1)}{2} = \dfrac{n+1}{2}\)

\(E\left(X^{2}\right) = \dfrac{1}{n}\displaystyle\sum_{x=1}^{n} x^{2} = \dfrac{1}{n} \cdot \dfrac{n(n+1)(2n+1)}{6} = \dfrac{(n+1)(2n+1)}{6}\)

\(\mathrm{Var}(X) = \dfrac{(n+1)(2n+1)}{6} - \dfrac{(n+1)^{2}}{4} = \dfrac{(n+1)\left[2(2n+1) - 3(n+1)\right]}{12} = \dfrac{(n+1)(n-1)}{12} = \dfrac{n^{2} - 1}{12}\)

\(\sigma = \sqrt{\dfrac{n^{2} - 1}{12}}\)

**(iv)** \(X = 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5\) with probabilities \(\dfrac{1}{32}, \dfrac{5}{32}, \dfrac{10}{32}, \dfrac{10}{32}, \dfrac{5}{32}, \dfrac{1}{32}\) (positive, sum \(= \dfrac{32}{32} = 1\)).

\(E(X) = \dfrac{0 + 5 + 20 + 30 + 20 + 5}{32} = \dfrac{80}{32} = \dfrac{5}{2} = 2.5\)

\(E\left(X^{2}\right) = \dfrac{0 + 5 + 40 + 90 + 80 + 25}{32} = \dfrac{240}{32} = \dfrac{15}{2} = 7.5\)

\(\mathrm{Var}(X) = \dfrac{15}{2} - \left(\dfrac{5}{2}\right)^{2} = \dfrac{30 - 25}{4} = \dfrac{5}{4} = 1.25\)

\(\sigma = \sqrt{\dfrac{5}{4}} = \dfrac{\sqrt{5}}{2} \approx 1.1180\)

**Answers.**

| Part | \(E(X)\) | \(\mathrm{Var}(X)\) | \(\sigma\) |
|---|---|---|---|
| (i) | \(\dfrac{11}{5} = 2.2\) | \(\dfrac{14}{25} = 0.56\) | \(\dfrac{\sqrt{14}}{5} \approx 0.7483\) |
| (ii) | \(\dfrac{1}{5} = 0.2\) | \(\dfrac{14}{25} = 0.56\) | \(\dfrac{\sqrt{14}}{5} \approx 0.7483\) |
| (iii) | \(\dfrac{n+1}{2}\) | \(\dfrac{n^{2}-1}{12}\) | \(\sqrt{\dfrac{n^{2}-1}{12}}\) |
| (iv) | \(\dfrac{5}{2} = 2.5\) | \(\dfrac{5}{4} = 1.25\) | \(\dfrac{\sqrt{5}}{2} \approx 1.1180\) |

Two coins are tossed, so the sample space is \(S = \{HH, HT, TH, TT\}\) with \(n(S) = 4\).

Let \(X\) be the amount (in rupees) won.

- 2 heads, i.e. \(HH\): wins ₹ 10, and \(P = \dfrac{1}{4}\)
- 1 head, i.e. \(HT\) or \(TH\): wins ₹ 5, and \(P = \dfrac{2}{4} = \dfrac{1}{2}\)
- no head, i.e. \(TT\): wins ₹ 2, and \(P = \dfrac{1}{4}\)

The probability distribution of the winning amount is

| \(X = x\) | 10 | 5 | 2 |
|---|---|---|---|
| \(P(X = x)\) | \(\dfrac{1}{4}\) | \(\dfrac{1}{2}\) | \(\dfrac{1}{4}\) |

All entries are positive and add to \(1\), so this is a valid p.m.f.

**Expected winning amount.**

\(E(X) = 10 \times \dfrac{1}{4} + 5 \times \dfrac{1}{2} + 2 \times \dfrac{1}{4} = \dfrac{10}{4} + \dfrac{10}{4} + \dfrac{2}{4} = \dfrac{22}{4} = \dfrac{11}{2} = 5.5\)

So the expected winning amount is ₹ 5.50.

**Variance.**

\(E\left(X^{2}\right) = 100 \times \dfrac{1}{4} + 25 \times \dfrac{1}{2} + 4 \times \dfrac{1}{4} = 25 + 12.5 + 1 = 38.5 = \dfrac{77}{2}\)

\(\mathrm{Var}(X) = E\left(X^{2}\right) - \left[E(X)\right]^{2} = \dfrac{77}{2} - \left(\dfrac{11}{2}\right)^{2} = \dfrac{154 - 121}{4} = \dfrac{33}{4} = 8.25\)

\(\sigma = \sqrt{\dfrac{33}{4}} = \dfrac{\sqrt{33}}{2} \approx 2.8723\)

\(\therefore\) the expected winning amount is \(\dfrac{11}{2} = 5.5\), i.e. ₹ 5.50, and the variance of the winning amount is \(\dfrac{33}{4} = 8.25\).

**First find \(k\).**

For a p.d.f. we need \(f(x) \geq 0\) everywhere **and** \(\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f(x)\,dx = 1\).

\(\int_{-2}^{2} k\left(4 - x^{2}\right)dx = k\left[4x - \dfrac{x^{3}}{3}\right]_{-2}^{2} = k\left[\left(8 - \dfrac{8}{3}\right) - \left(-8 + \dfrac{8}{3}\right)\right] = k \times \dfrac{32}{3}\)

\(\dfrac{32k}{3} = 1\), so \(k = \dfrac{3}{32}\).

Since \(k > 0\) and \(4 - x^{2} \geq 0\) for \(-2 \leq x \leq 2\), we have \(f(x) \geq 0\) throughout, so both conditions hold and \(f\) is a genuine p.d.f.

**(i) \(P(X > 0)\).**

\(P(X > 0) = \int_{0}^{2} \dfrac{3}{32}\left(4 - x^{2}\right)dx = \dfrac{3}{32}\left[4x - \dfrac{x^{3}}{3}\right]_{0}^{2} = \dfrac{3}{32}\left(8 - \dfrac{8}{3}\right) = \dfrac{3}{32} \times \dfrac{16}{3} = \dfrac{1}{2}\)

This is what we should expect: \(f\) is an even function, so the distribution is symmetric about \(0\).

**(ii) \(P(-1 < X < 1)\).**

\(P(-1 < X < 1) = \dfrac{3}{32}\left[4x - \dfrac{x^{3}}{3}\right]_{-1}^{1} = \dfrac{3}{32}\left[\left(4 - \dfrac{1}{3}\right) - \left(-4 + \dfrac{1}{3}\right)\right] = \dfrac{3}{32} \times \dfrac{22}{3} = \dfrac{22}{32} = \dfrac{11}{16}\)

**(iii)** As printed, "\(X < 0.5\) or \(X > 0.5\)" covers every real number except the single point \(x = 0.5\), and \(P(X = 0.5) = 0\) because \(X\) is continuous, so read literally the answer is \(1\); the intended question is almost certainly the symmetric one, \(P(X < -0.5 \text{ or } X > 0.5)\), which is worked out below.

\(P(-0.5 < X < 0.5) = \dfrac{3}{32}\left[4x - \dfrac{x^{3}}{3}\right]_{-1/2}^{1/2} = \dfrac{3}{32} \times 2\left(2 - \dfrac{1}{24}\right) = \dfrac{3}{32} \times \dfrac{47}{12} = \dfrac{47}{128}\)

\(\therefore\ P(X < -0.5 \text{ or } X > 0.5) = 1 - \dfrac{47}{128} = \dfrac{81}{128}\)

\(\therefore\ k = \dfrac{3}{32}\); (i) \(\dfrac{1}{2}\); (ii) \(\dfrac{11}{16}\); (iii) \(\dfrac{81}{128}\) on the intended symmetric reading, and \(1\) if the stem is taken exactly as printed.

Here \(f(x) = \dfrac{1}{2a}\) for \(0 < x < 2a\), and \(f(x) = 0\) otherwise.

Throughout we take \(a > 0\). This is needed twice: it makes \((0, 2a)\) a genuine interval and makes \(f(x) = \dfrac{1}{2a} > 0\) there, and it puts both \(\dfrac{a}{2}\) and \(\dfrac{3a}{2}\) inside the range, since \(0 < \dfrac{a}{2} < \dfrac{3a}{2} < 2a\).

**Check that \(f\) is a p.d.f.**

\(\int_{0}^{2a} \dfrac{1}{2a}\,dx = \dfrac{1}{2a}\left[x\right]_{0}^{2a} = \dfrac{2a}{2a} = 1\)

and \(f(x) \geq 0\) everywhere, so \(X\) is uniformly distributed over \((0, 2a)\).

**The left tail.**

\(P\left(X < \dfrac{a}{2}\right) = \int_{0}^{a/2} \dfrac{1}{2a}\,dx = \dfrac{1}{2a}\left[x\right]_{0}^{a/2} = \dfrac{1}{2a} \times \dfrac{a}{2} = \dfrac{1}{4}\)

**The right tail.**

\(P\left(X > \dfrac{3a}{2}\right) = \int_{3a/2}^{2a} \dfrac{1}{2a}\,dx = \dfrac{1}{2a}\left[x\right]_{3a/2}^{2a} = \dfrac{1}{2a}\left(2a - \dfrac{3a}{2}\right) = \dfrac{1}{2a} \times \dfrac{a}{2} = \dfrac{1}{4}\)

\(\therefore\ P\left(X < \dfrac{a}{2}\right) = P\left(X > \dfrac{3a}{2}\right) = \dfrac{1}{4}\), as required.

**Remark.** The common value \(\dfrac{1}{4}\) is free of \(a\), and this is easy to see directly: the intervals \(\left(0, \dfrac{a}{2}\right)\) and \(\left(\dfrac{3a}{2}, 2a\right)\) both have length \(\dfrac{a}{2}\), which is one quarter of the total length \(2a\), and for a uniform density the probability is proportional to length.

**To determine \(k\).**

For a p.d.f., \(\int_{0}^{4} f(x)\,dx = 1\):

\(\int_{0}^{4} \dfrac{k}{\sqrt{x}}\,dx = k\int_{0}^{4} x^{-1/2}\,dx = k\left[2\sqrt{x}\right]_{0}^{4} = k(2 \times 2 - 0) = 4k\)

\(4k = 1\), so \(k = \dfrac{1}{4}\).

Since \(k > 0\) and \(\sqrt{x} > 0\) on \((0, 4)\), we have \(f(x) > 0\) there, so both p.d.f. conditions hold. (The integral converges even though \(f(x) \to \infty\) as \(x \to 0^{+}\).)

**The c.d.f.**

For \(0 < x < 4\),

\(F(x) = \int_{0}^{x} \dfrac{1}{4\sqrt{t}}\,dt = \dfrac{1}{4}\left[2\sqrt{t}\right]_{0}^{x} = \dfrac{2\sqrt{x}}{4} = \dfrac{\sqrt{x}}{2}\)

Hence

\(F(x) = \begin{cases} 0, & x \leq 0 \\ \dfrac{\sqrt{x}}{2}, & 0 < x < 4 \\ 1, & x \geq 4 \end{cases}\)

The three pieces fit together correctly, since \(\dfrac{\sqrt{4}}{2} = 1\), and \(F\) is increasing, as a c.d.f. must be.

**The two probabilities.**

\(P(X \leq 2) = F(2) = \dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \approx 0.7071\)

\(P(X \leq 1) = F(1) = \dfrac{\sqrt{1}}{2} = \dfrac{1}{2} = 0.5\)

\(\therefore\ k = \dfrac{1}{4}\); \(F(x) = \dfrac{\sqrt{x}}{2}\) for \(0 < x < 4\) (with \(F(x) = 0\) below and \(F(x) = 1\) above); \(P(X \leq 2) = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \approx 0.7071\) and \(P(X \leq 1) = \dfrac{1}{2}\).
